title: Pupils plant a green wall against the waves
text:
Last Saturday, ninety pupils from SD Harapan Pesisir waded into the mud of their village coast to plant five hundred mangrove seedlings. The event, which lasted from seven in the morning until noon, was the school's biggest environmental project so far.

Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water along tropical shores. Their tangled roots rise above the mud, and they do two valuable jobs. First, they slow down waves, which helps to protect the coastline from erosion. Second, their roots trap soil, and the shady water between them shelters young fish, shrimps and crabs. Many local families earn their living from fishing, so a healthy mangrove forest means more fish.

The headteacher, Pak Budi, explained why the school took on the task. "Over the past twenty years, the shoreline behind our school has moved inland by about thirty metres," he said. "The sea took the old football field. Now we want the children to see that they can do something about it."

The planting was carefully organised. Each pupil received one seedling, which had been grown in a nursery for six months, and a bamboo stick to mark its place. The older children dug holes, the younger ones set the seedlings in the mud, and everyone pressed the soil firmly around the roots. A group of fishermen showed the pupils where to plant, so that the young trees would not be washed away at high tide.

Not everyone was sure the plan would work. A few villagers pointed out that half of the seedlings from a previous project had died, probably because they were planted too low in the water. This time, the organisers say, the locations were chosen with great care. The school will also check on the trees every month and replace any that have failed.

"My seedling is called Gajah," said Sekar, aged ten, holding up her muddy hands. "It is the biggest one, and I think it will live."

Scientists estimate that the new trees will take three to five years to grow thick enough to protect the shore properly. The school plans to hold its next planting day in September, and is inviting neighbouring villages to take part.
